TempBench · overnight run · 26 July 2026

Hunting a task where reading a window of tokens beats reading one

Dictionaries were trained this time — the paper's own five architectures, at matched code budget, with three seeds and an untrained control for every cell. The headline finding of the first few hours turned out to be an artefact, was caught by a check, and was retracted before it reached this page. What survived is smaller and real.

The false positive, first

What I nearly reported

The claim that failed. On tokens since the text switched source document, the paper's TXC at T=8 scored 0.294 against 0.139 for the per-token SAE — a 6σ gap over three seeds, beating T-SAE and Stacked SAE too, at matched code budget. Every automatic check passed.

Why it was wrong. A linear probe on the raw activation at the single label position — no dictionary at all — reaches r = 0.31–0.37 on that task. Higher than any trained dictionary. So the signal was never non-local; the per-token dictionary simply discarded more of it. The comparison was real but it measures code efficiency at matched sparsity, not temporal structure, and presenting it as the latter would have been the central claim of the paper resting on a mislabelled quantity.

What changed as a result. A raw-activation gate now runs before any dictionary training, and a task only qualifies if a dimension-matched window average beats a single position on the raw activations. That test is cheap and it reorders the candidate list completely.

The gate that decides what is worth training

Which labels actually need more than one position?

All three probes below run on the same rows, on raw activations. Window-mean is the honest comparison to single position: it has the same number of features, so neither is favoured by dimensionality. The flattened window is shown too, and it is worse everywhere — a fixed-budget probe on T×768 features degrades as T grows, which is exactly the trap that makes naive window-versus-token comparisons unreliable.

The pattern is consistent and it matches what the earlier relational work predicted: trailing rates — quantities accumulated over many tokens — genuinely need a window, and the gain grows with window size. Clocks (tokens since the last switch, tokens since the last speaker change) do not: the model already carries them on the current token.

These numbers are reproducible and the architecture ordering is real. What they cannot support is the claim that a window exposes something a single position lacks, because on this task the raw single position scores higher than every dictionary here. Read as a statement about how much signal each code retains at equal sparsity, the ordering is still interesting — TXC-post retains roughly twice what the per-token SAE does — but that is a different claim and a weaker one.

The material

What the winning task actually asks for, on real text

The label is the rate at which new word types appear over the preceding span, with the document-position trend removed (novelty falls through any document simply because vocabulary gets used up, and that trend is subtracted so it cannot be read off position). Two real windows from the same FineWeb document, 32 tokens each, ending at the position the probe reads. N marks a token that is the first occurrence of its type in the document.

What “trailing” means, exactly

The label at token t is

label[t] = sum over lags l = 1..64 of  w[l] * novel[t-l]

  novel[t-l] = 1 if the token 64..1 places back was the FIRST
               occurrence of its word type in this document, else 0
  w[l]       proportional to 2^(-l/16), normalised to sum to 1
             so a token 16 back counts half as much as one 1 back,
             32 back a quarter, and the sum cuts off at 64

Three consequences worth being explicit about. The current token contributes nothing — lags start at 1, so the label is never a property of the token being read. The label is undefined for the first 64 tokens of a document, and those rows are excluded. And a dictionary with window T can only see part of it: a 4-token window covers 17% of the weight, 8 covers 31%, 16 covers 53%, 32 covers 80%. That is the direct reason a wider window has more to gain here, and it is why this is a state-tracking task rather than a word-recognition one.

The version used for the headline, nov_resid, additionally subtracts the average rate for that position-in-document bin, because novelty falls through any document as vocabulary gets used up — without that subtraction a probe could score well by reading position alone.

busy — many new words

Whitehead 14. Kurt Baptiste 15. Clay Priest 16. Dave Taylor 17. Luke Bateman 18. Michael Oldfield 19. Jeff Lima Dylan Edwards 2
NNN.NNNN.NN..NNN.NNNN.NNNN.NNNN.
label at this position
trailing novelty rate 0.764, after removing the position trend +0.406

quiet — mostly repeats

rin, who may return from a knee injury after he was named on the extended bench. If the Panthers are to prevail on Sunday, it will be their defence
N.N.........N..NN.N....N.......N
label at this position
trailing novelty rate 0.256, after removing the position trend -0.178

This is why a single position cannot answer it and why the answer is not a word property: the same word can be new or a repeat depending on what came before, and the quantity asked for is a rate over roughly the last few dozen tokens. A raw probe confirms the asymmetry — a dimension-matched window average scores 0.725 against 0.572 for the single position.

Reproducing it end to end

# 0. interface check (seconds)
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.smoke

# 1. cache activations for every committed label pack (gpt2: ~1 min)
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.sweep cache \
    --model gpt2 --layer 6

# 2. the gate: which tasks need more than one position?
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.rawgate \
    --model gpt2 --layer 6 --t-ladder 4,16

# 3. the headline panel (gpt2, ~40 min)
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.focus \
    --task novelty_resid --model gpt2 --steps 4000 \
    --seeds 1,2,42 --t-ladder 4,8,16,32 --match nnz --tag focus_novresid

# 4. the same on the paper's subject model
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.focus \
    --task novelty_resid --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B \
    --layer 12 --steps 2500 --seeds 1,2,42 --t-ladder 4,8,16 \
    --d-sae 8192 --match nnz --tag focus_nov_8b

# 5. audit the claims, then figures and this page
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.audit --pattern 'focus_*.json'
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.viz_focus --tag focus_novresid
.venv/bin/python -m experiments.explorations.txcwin.report

Training

optimiser
Adam, no weight decay, no learning-rate schedule
learning rate
3e-4 (constant)
loss
each architecture's own train_step — the repo's registered implementation, unmodified. BatchTopK for the per-token/Stacked/TXC family; T-SAE adds its matryoshka groups and its contrastive pair term
windows
sampled uniformly at random from the whole cache each step; T-SAE trains on 8-token sequences because its contrastive term needs a consecutive pair, then is read per token
precision
activations cached in float16, cast to float32 for training
architecture source
resolved from configs/archs.yaml at run time, so a class rename cannot silently change the panel
untrained control
identical construction and seed, zero training steps, same probe and rows

Code budget calibration

Nominal k buys different amounts per architecture, so it is calibrated per (architecture, T) by binary search until the number of non-zero code entries the probe sees is within 0.12 of the target, measured on 256 held-out windows after a short warm-up. The achieved value is recorded in every cell as l0 and the audit rejects any comparison where the two sides differ by more than 2x. At T=8 nominal k=20 yields 20.0 non-zeros for the per-token SAE and TXC-post, 19.8 for Stacked, but 114 for TXC-pre.

Read-out and scoring

what the probe sees
one code vector per row. TXC returns a single shared code for the window; the others return one code per position and the position carrying the label is taken. This is the repo's per-tile convention and it equalises code bandwidth
probe
ridge regression, penalty 1.0, on train-set standardised features; scalar labels scored by held-out Pearson r, binary labels by rank AUC
train/test split
by DOCUMENT (0.8 of documents to train), so no document appears in both halves and a probe cannot win by memorising a passage
confidence intervals
300 bootstrap resamples of the test rows per cell; across seeds, the reported +/- is the sample standard deviation and significance uses the seed-level standard error
degeneracy guards
a cell is rejected if the label is flat on test, if fewer than 50 rows fall on either side of the split, if the dictionary has no active latents, or if the probe predicts a constant

Data

Token streams and labels are the committed exact-label packs under experiments/explorations/task_hunt/labels/ (76 MB, built earlier in this project, not by this run): a pinned 400-document FineWeb sample and a 5,000-dialogue DailyDialog sample, with labels computed mechanically from the text — no judge, no API. Activation caches live outside the repo at /workspace/txcwin_caches/ (float16 memmaps, ~18 GB) and regenerate from the committed code plus those token ids; caches are keyed by a hash of the token stream so label packs sharing a stream share one cache. Every number on this page comes from experiments/explorations/txcwin/results/*.json, which are committed.

Limits

What this still is not

  • A triage harness, not the canonical pipeline. Training happens in-process rather than through the project's canonical runner, so none of these numbers are on the leaderboard and none carry a code-version stamp. Whatever survives has to be re-run properly before it is a result.
  • Small dictionaries. d_sae = 2048 with k = 20 on gpt2, against the paper's 18432 at k = 20. Expansion factor is the single most likely thing to change the ordering.
  • One layer, one corpus per task. Layer 6 of gpt2 on a pinned 400-document fineweb sample and a 5,000-dialogue sample.
  • The T=4 collapse is unexplained. It affects every window architecture and their untrained controls, so it is a property of the rows or the window construction rather than of training, and I have not found it.
  • MLC and TFA are absent. MLC needs several layers cached at once; TFA is not in this repo's registry. Both are in the paper's panel.
Reviewer bbby, question 5

Parameter counts, inference cost, and training cost per architecture

Counted by instantiating each registered class at the paper's own hyperparameters, so these cannot drift from the code. FLOPs are analytic at 2 per multiply-accumulate, with a sparse decode (the honest number: a dense decode would be d_sae/k = 900× larger and no implementation does that). Per-token cost assumes windows tile the sequence, which is what the paper's one-code-per-tile evaluation implies; at stride 1 a window architecture would cost T× more.

The short answer

A temporal crosscoder costs 5× the parameters of a per-token SAE at equal width, and the same FLOPs per token. The parameters go into T separate encoder and decoder matrices; the FLOPs are identical because one window pass covers T tokens. MLC is the expensive one on both axes — it reads five layers at a single position, so nothing is amortised: 5× the parameters and 5× the FLOPs, reaching 8% of a full forward pass of gemma-2-2b.

And the reviewer is right about T-SAE — more right than they knew

T-SAE is registered at d_sae = 16384 while every other architecture uses 18432: 11% narrower, 75.5M parameters against 85.0M on the probing model. But the backtracking section is worse. There, topk_sae, batchtopk_sae and txc_base all receive a per-section override to d_sae = 32768 — and T-SAE has no override, so it silently stays at 16384. In the paper's headline backtracking comparison T-SAE runs at half the dictionary width and half the parameters of the architecture it is being compared against (134.2M vs 268.5M), and the mismatch favours the paper's own architecture. That needs either a matched re-run or an explicit statement in the text; it cannot stay implicit.

The mechanism

Why temporal crosscoders lose almost everywhere — and the shape of the tasks where they do not

The reason, in one line: attention already did the job, and it is strong

A transformer's attention aggregates across positions and writes the result onto the current token. Anything the model needs in order to predict the next token is therefore available locally, at every position, almost immediately. A dictionary that reads one token gets that aggregation for free; a dictionary that reads a window has nothing left to contribute. The window architecture is not weak — it is redundant with a mechanism the model runs constantly.

This is measured, not asserted. On four relational labels — subject–verb agreement, factual consistency, labelled provenance, marker nesting — a probe on a single position goes from chance at the embeddings to 1.000 by layer 1–4. At the embeddings, before any attention has run, only a reader that mixes positions can answer (0.994 against 0.488 for every additive readout, a gap of +0.49). One attention layer later every reader is perfect. The architectural advantage is real and it has almost nowhere to live.

The operational test, so this stops being a guessing game

Before training any dictionary, probe the raw activations twice on identical rows: once at the single label position, once on the dimension-matched average of the window. If the window average does not beat the single position, attention has already localised the signal and no window architecture can win — skip the task. If it does, the gap is the headroom a window dictionary is competing for. That check costs minutes, needs no training, and it reordered this project's candidate list completely: every clock failed it, every trailing rate passed.

Two design rules follow. Pick labels whose support is much longer than one token and which the model has no reason to resolve into an answer. And report the coverage number: a window of T tokens sees a known fraction of the label's support (17% at T=4, 31% at T=8, 53% at T=16, 80% at T=32 for the label used here), which turns the T-curve into a prediction rather than a sweep.

What this says about the paper. The small margins on sparse probing, emergent misalignment and HH-RLHF are not a failure of the architecture; they are what the mechanism predicts, because those targets are per-token-available. The backtracking result is not luck either — it is the one task in the panel with the right shape. What was missing was a way to tell the two apart in advance, and the raw gate is that.
